overview.body:
**Niamh** (*niamh*) ​— Beauty, Otherworld ‌· Bright, ‌radiant — is ​the golden-haired daughter ​of the king ​of Tír na ​nÓg who ​rides out of ‌the western sea ​on a white ​horse to claim ‌[[oisin|Oisín]], the ​last great poet ‌of the Fianna, ​and carries him ‌to the ​Land of Youth, ​where three hundred ​years pass as ​a single season. ​Her story ‌survives as one ​beloved tale: the ‌*Laoi Oisín ar ​Thír na ‌nÓg*, 'The Lay ​of Oisín in ‌the Land of ​Youth', ascribed to ‌the eighteenth-century ​poet Mícheál Coimín ​and first printed ‌with an English ‌translation by the ‌Ossianic Society ​in 1859.[^1]

The ​name is the ‌Irish common noun ​made personal: ​Old Irish *niam*, ‌'lustre, brilliance, radiance', ​so that Niamh ​is simply 'the ‌radiant one' ​— and the ‌lay wears the ​meaning on its ​sleeve in her ​epithet, *Chinn ​Óir*, 'of the ‌Golden Hair'.[^2] Late ‌tradition makes her ​a daughter ‌of [[manannan|Manannán mac ​Lir]], lord of ​the sea-Otherworlds; the ‌lay itself names ‌her father ‌only as the ‌king of Tír ​na nÓg, and ‌the Manannán paternity ​is the ​tradition's own harmonization.[^3]

​PuniCodex restores the ‌name as **Niamh** ​— identical ​to the ASCII ​input, because the ‌canonical modern Irish ​spelling writes no ​diacritic. The ​mechanical rule therefore ‌places it in ​Tier 2: nothing ‌distinctive is ​lost in transit, ‌a statement about ​orthography and never ‌about the figure. ‌No domain ​is claimed: the ​plain-ASCII **niamh.com** is ​registered to a ​third party outside ‌the collection ‌and is watched ​for release.

MacKillop, James, A Dictionary of Celtic Mythology (Oxford: Oxford University Press, 1998), s.v. Niamh, Manannán mac Lir.

the-name.body:
The name ​is attested in ‌Old and Middle ‌Irish as **Níam** ​— the medieval ​spelling, with the ​síneadh fada marking ​the long vowel ​— and in ‌canonical modern Irish ​as **Niamh**, where ​the digraph mh ‌writes the lenited ​m and the ‌fada is dropped.[^1] ​It is ‌the common noun ​made personal: eDIL's ​first *niam* is ​'lustre, brilliance, radiance', ​and the name ​is the abstract ‌quality carried by ​a woman — ‌'the radiant one'.[^1] ​The lay itself ‌makes the equation ​visible, styling her ‌*Niamh Chinn Óir*, ​'Niamh of the ‌Golden Hair': the ​brightness of the ​name worn as ‌an epithet.[^2]

She ‌is not the ‌only bearer of ​the name in ​the corpus — ‌Irish tradition knew ​several women called ​Niamh, among them ‌a wife of ​Conall Cernach in ​the Ulster Cycle ‌— but ​the golden-haired rider ‌of the Fenian ​lay has absorbed ​the name so ​completely that in ​the modern imagination ‌there is only ‌one.[^3]

The ASCII ​form *niamh* loses ‌nothing, because the ​canonical modern Irish ​spelling is already ‌plain Latin letters; ‌the restoration is ‌therefore a matter ‌of canonical reference, ​not rescued diacritics, ‌and the name ​is classified Tier ​2 by the ​project's mechanical rule.

‌The letter-by-letter transformation ​runs:

- **n** ​→ **N** — ​Same, capitalized
- ‌**i** → **i** ​— Same
- ​**a** → **a** ​— Same
‌- **m** → ​**m** — Same
‌- **h** → ​**h** — Same

‌The project holds ​no domain for ‌this name: **niamh.com** ‌is registered to ​a third party ​outside the PuniCodex ​collection and is ​watched for release. ‌The temple lives ‌at its canonical ​lexicon address.

pronunciation.body:
The pronunciation ​of the ‌name in modern ‌Irish is **/ˈn̠ʲiːəvˠ/** ​— Modern ​Irish (Standard).[^1]

Phoneme ​by phoneme:

- ​**N-** — ​Slender (palatalized) dental ‌nasal [n̠ʲ], the ​'ny' of ​'new' in an ‌Irish accent; Irish ​n before ‌i is always ​slender
- **-ia-** ‌— Long ​close [iː] releasing ​into a ​brief [ə]; Munster ​Irish sounds both ​beats, 'NEE-uv', ‌while the standard ​northern pronunciation draws ‌them into ​one long syllable, ‌'NEEV'
- **-mh** ​— The ‌lenited m of ​Irish spelling, sounded ‌as broad ​[vˠ], a soft ​'v'; the h ‌writes the ‌lenition and is ‌never an ​'h' sound

For ​the modern speaker, ‌the closest ​approximation is: 'NEE-uv' ​(Munster) or 'NEEV' ‌(standard) — ​the weight on ​the long 'ee', ‌the final ​mh a soft ‌v; never 'nee-AM' ​and never ​an English h.

​Kindred and historical ​forms of ‌the name:

- ‌**Old Irish** — ​Níam, the ‌medieval spelling, beside ​the common ​noun niam, 'lustre, ‌brilliance'
- **The ‌name as ‌word** — niam ‌(eDIL s.v. 1 ​niam), 'lustre, ‌brilliance, radiance' — ​the name is ​the abstract ​noun made personal
‌- **Other bearers** ​— Niamh, ​wife of Conall ​Cernach of the ‌Ulster Cycle
​- **Modern Irish** ​— Niamh, ​among the most ‌popular Irish girls' ​names of ‌the modern era[^2]

​Niamh is Tier ‌2 because ​the restoration preserves ‌nothing ASCII loses: ‌the letters ​of the canonical ​modern spelling are ​the letters ​of the keyboard. ‌The capital alone ‌marks the ​temple form.

sources.citation: Ó Siadhail, Mícheál, Modern Irish: Grammatical Structure and Dialectal Variation (Cambridge: Cambridge University Press, 1989), on slender consonants, lenition, and dialectal vocalism.
Dictionary of the Irish Language (Dublin: Royal Irish Academy, 1913–76; electronic ed. eDIL 2019), s.v. 1 niam.

domains.body:
**Niamh** is ​catalogued under ‌the domain 'Beauty, ‌Otherworld' — ​the two ​words the whole ​lay is ​built from.[^1]

### ​Beauty

She ‌enters the ​story as the ​most beautiful ‌woman Oisín has ​ever seen, ‌and the ​lay gives the ‌claim a ​name to match: ​*niam*, 'radiance', ​and the ​epithet *Chinn Óir*, ​'of the ‌Golden Hair'. Hers ​is the ‌Otherworld's beauty — ​the kind ‌that crosses ​the sea to ‌do its ​own choosing, praises ‌the mortal ​above every ​man present, and ‌is not ‌refused.[^1]

### Otherworld

‌She is ​the daughter ​of the king ‌of Tír ​na nÓg, the ​Land of ‌the Young ​across the western ​sea, where ‌age, sickness, and ​decay never ‌come; and she ​is its ​ferryman — ​the white horse ​that rides ‌the sea-road as ‌if it ​were a ‌road answers to ​her. In ​her person the ‌Irish Otherworld ‌does what ‌it does in ‌[[midir|Midir]] and ​[[etain|Étaín]], in Connla's ‌crystal ship, ​and in ​Bran's silver branch: ​it issues ‌an invitation.[^2]

### ​The Time-Bargain

​Her domain has ​a third ‌face the ​lexicon's two words ​hold between ​them: time. Three ‌hundred years ​in Tír ‌na nÓg cost ​Oisín nothing ‌until he touched ​Irish soil ‌— and ‌then they cost ​him everything ​at once. Niamh ​keeps the ​boundary where ‌the Otherworld's exemption ‌and mortality's ​arithmetic meet.[^1]

sources.citation: O'Daly, John, ed. and trans., 'The Lay of Oisin in the Land of the Young', Transactions of the Ossianic Society 4 (1859).
Mac Cana, Proinsias, Celtic Mythology (London: Hamlyn, 1970), on the Irish Otherworld and its invitations.

symbols.body:
Niamh's attributes ​are the ‌properties of ‌the lay ​itself — ​a horse, ​a head ​of golden hair, ​a sea-road, ‌and the ​single prohibition ​that ends ‌them all:[^1]

​- **The ‌white horse** — ​The Otherworld's ‌transport, which ​carries [[oisin|Oisín]] ​to Tír ​na nÓg ​and home again; ​the lay ‌leaves it ​unnamed, and ‌later tradition ​gives it ‌[[manannan|Manannán]]'s horse, ​Enbarr — it ‌is also ​the vehicle ‌of the ​warning: touch ​the ground ‌and all ‌is lost
- ‌**The golden ​hair** — ​*Chinn Óir*, ‌'of the ​Golden Head': ​the name ‌Niamh, 'radiance', worn ​as an ​epithet — ‌brightness made ​visible
- ‌**The sea-crossing** ​— The threshold ​between the ​mortal world ​and Tír ‌na nÓg, ‌ridden as ​if it ‌were a road; ​the passage ​where the ‌lay sets ‌its unexplained ‌marvels — ‌the red-eared ​hound, the golden ‌apple, the ​pursuing rider
​- **The ​three hundred ‌years** — ​Time suspended ​in the Land ​of Youth: ‌the Otherworld's ​gift and ​its price, ​counted only ‌when it is ​spent
- ‌**The broken ​girth** — ‌The saddle-strap ​that snaps ‌over the ‌flagstone in the ​Irish glen: ​the single ​touch of ​home soil ‌that resumes ‌mortality in ​an instant[^2]

sources.citation: O'Daly, John, ed. and trans., 'The Lay of Oisin in the Land of the Young', Transactions of the Ossianic Society 4 (1859).
MacKillop, James, A Dictionary of Celtic Mythology (Oxford: Oxford University Press, 1998), s.v. Niamh, Oisín.

mythology.body:
Niamh's mythology is a ​single arc — summons, crossing, sojourn, ‌longing, fall — told in one late ‌and beloved text, the *Laoi Oisín ​ar Thír na nÓg*, and framed at ​its end by the medieval Oisín-and-Patrick tradition.[^1]

​### The Summons from over the ​Sea (Laoi Oisín ar Thír na nÓg)

​A maiden none of the Fianna ‌knows rides out of the west on ​a white horse and names herself: ​Niamh Chinn Óir, daughter of the king ‌of Tír na nÓg. She has heard ​the fame of [[oisin|Oisín]] across the ‌sea and has come for his love, ​and her praise of him rises ‌above every man of the Fianna present. ​Oisín answers that he has never ​seen her equal, gives his word, and ​mounts behind her.[^1]

### The Wonders on ​the Wave

The white horse rides ​the sea as if it were a ‌road, and marvels pass them on ​the wave: a fawn coursed by a ‌white hound with red ears; a ​maiden riding with a golden apple in ‌her hand; a young rider in a ​crimson cloak hard behind her, a ‌gold-hilted sword at his side. Oisín asks ​what they mean, and the lay ‌lets them pass unexplained — the old ​heraldry of the síd, set loose ​on the open sea.[^1]

### Three Hundred ‌Years as a Dream

In the Land ‌of Youth the king receives Oisín, ‌and he and Niamh are made one. ​There is no age there and ​no decay; Niamh bears him three children, ‌named at his asking for the ​world he left — the sons Fionn ​and Oscar, for his father [[fionn|Fionn]] and ‌his son, and the daughter Plúr ​na mBan, 'flower of women'. Three hundred ​years go by, sweet as a ‌single season.[^1]

### The Warning and the ​Horse

Longing comes on Oisín at ‌last — to see Ireland, to look ​for Fionn and the remnant of ​the Fianna. Niamh does not refuse him. ​She gives him the white horse and ​the command on which everything turns: ‌ride where he will, but he must ‌not dismount, for if his foot ​touches the soil of Ireland he will ‌never return to the Land of ​Youth.[^1]

### The Slab in the Glen

​Ireland is changed past recognition: the Fianna ‌are gone, their ramparts green mounds, ‌the people small, and Christianity has come. ‌In a glen of the south ‌— the lay names Gleann an Smóil ​— Oisín finds men straining at ‌a great flagstone that one man of ​the Fianna would have lifted alone; leaning ​from the saddle to help, he ​puts his strength to the stone, and ‌the girth breaks. His foot touches ​Irish soil, the three hundred years land ​on him at once, and he ​rises an old, withered, grey-haired man while ‌the white horse wheels home over the ​sea without him.[^1]

### The Old ​Man and the Saint (Acallam na Senórach ​/ the after-tradition)

The lay ends ‌where the medieval tradition had long stationed ​Oisín: at the door of St. ‌Patrick. The *Acallam na Senórach* (c. 1200) ​already framed its Fenian treasury this way ‌— Oisín and Caílte, the last ​of the Fianna, walking Ireland with Patrick ‌and reciting its lore. The Niamh ‌episode belongs to the later lay, not ​to the Acallam, but the ending ​is one: the pagan hero out of ​time, telling the golden age to the ​new faith. Niamh remains in Tír ‌na nÓg with their children, on the ‌far side of a sea he ​will never cross again.[^2]

sources.citation: O'Daly, John, ed. and trans., 'The Lay of Oisin in the Land of the Young, ascribed to Micle Coimin', Transactions of the Ossianic Society 4 (Dublin: The Ossianic Society, 1859).
Stokes, Whitley, ed. and trans., 'Acallamh na Senórach', Irische Texte, ser. 4, vol. 1 (Leipzig: Hirzel, 1900).

syncretism.body:
Niamh belongs ​to the ‌oldest company ‌in Irish narrative: ​the Otherworld ​woman who comes ​for a ​mortal man. ​*Echtrae Chonnlai* gives ‌the type ​its starkest form ​— a ‌woman of ​the síd, visible ‌only to ​Connla, throws him ‌an apple ​that never ​diminishes and calls ​him to ​Mag Mell, until ​he leaps ‌into her ​crystal ship and ‌is seen ​no more.[^1] *Immram ‌Brain* sends ​a woman ‌from Emain with ​a silver ‌branch to summon ​Bran across ​the sea ‌to the Land ‌of Women, ‌where a year ​is no ​time at ‌all — the ​same time-arithmetic ​as Oisín's three ‌centuries.[^1] In ​*Tochmarc Étaíne* ​the direction reverses: ‌[[midir|Midir]] of ​Brí Léith wins ‌back [[etain|Étaín]], ​and the ​two fly from ​Tara as ​swans.[^2]

The frame ‌late tradition ‌gave Niamh ​herself is genealogical: ‌she is ​made a daughter ​of [[manannan|Manannán ‌mac Lir]], ‌lord of the ‌sea-Otherworlds Emain ‌Ablach and Mag ​Mell, whose ‌Welsh cognate ​is [[manawydan|Manawydan fab ​Llŷr]] — ​though the lay ‌names her ​father only ​as the king ​of Tír ‌na nÓg, and ​the Manannán ​paternity is ​the tradition's own ‌harmonization.[^3] Folklore ​comparison adds the ‌international motif: ​the supernatural ‌lapse of time ​in fairyland ‌— the traveller ‌who returns ​to find ​centuries gone — ​which Hartland ​made the type-case ‌of The ‌Science of ​Fairy Tales.[^4]

sources.citation: Meyer, Kuno, and Alfred Nutt, ed. and trans., The Voyage of Bran, Son of Febal, 2 vols. (London: David Nutt, 1895–97), including Echtrae Chonnlai.
Bergin, Osborn, and R. I. Best, ed. and trans., 'Tochmarc Étaíne', Ériu 12 (1938), 137–196.

Hartland, Edwin Sidney, The Science of Fairy Tales: An Inquiry into Fairy Mythology (London: Walter Scott, 1891), the chapter on the supernatural lapse of time in Fairyland.

cultural-legacy.body:
Niamh has ​the largest ‌modern afterlife ‌of any ​Irish Otherworld woman, ​and it ​runs through ​one poem. ​W. B. Yeats's ‌*The Wanderings ​of Oisin* ​(1889) — ‌his first major ​work and ‌a foundation-poem ​of the ‌Irish Literary Revival ​— took ​the lay's ​summons as ​its frame: Niamh ​calls Oisin ‌away on ​the white ‌horse, and three ​enchanted islands ‌later he ​returns to ‌a Christian Ireland ​and dies ‌with the ​Fianna on ​his lips. Yeats's ‌three islands ‌are his ‌own invention, ​but the wooer ​is the ‌lay's, and ​through him ​Niamh became world ‌literature's type ​of the ​Celtic Otherworld ‌bride.[^1] Lady Gregory's ​Gods and ‌Fighting Men ​(1904) carried ​the prose retelling ​to the ​same generation.[^2]

‌In Ireland ‌itself the name ​went the ‌opposite way ​— from ​mythology to the ‌birth register. ‌Niamh became ‌one of ‌the most popular ​Irish girls' ‌names of ​the late ​twentieth century, so ​that the ‌golden-haired rider ​is now, ​for most who ​bear the ‌name, simply ​themselves. And ​Tír na nÓg ​has passed ‌into the ​general vocabulary ‌as the default ​name of ‌the Celtic ​paradise: the ‌land over the ‌western sea ​where nobody ​grows old, ​reached only on ​a white ‌horse, and ‌only in ​her company.[^3]

sources.citation: Yeats, W. B., The Wanderings of Oisin and Other Poems (London: Kegan Paul, Trench, 1889).
Gregory, Lady Augusta, Gods and Fighting Men (London: John Murray, 1904).
Koch, John T., ed., Celtic Culture: A Historical Encyclopedia, 5 vols. (Santa Barbara: ABC-CLIO, 2006), s.v. Niamh, Tír na nÓg.

archaeology.body:
Niamh is ​an entirely ‌textual figure: ‌no ogham ​stone names ​her, no ​votive deposit ​invokes her, ​and Irish ‌paganism generally ​left literature ​rather than ‌dedications.[^1] Her ​tale has ‌an exact ​documentary trail. ‌The *Laoi ​Oisín ar ​Thír na ​nÓg*, ascribed ​to the ​eighteenth-century Clare ‌poet Mícheál ​Coimín, survives ‌in the ​Irish paper-manuscript ‌tradition and ​reached print ‌in the ​Transactions of ‌the Ossianic ​Society (vol. ​4, 1859) ‌— the ‌learned society ‌that did ​for the ​Fenian lays ‌what the ​Grimms did ​for the ‌folktale.[^2]

The ​medieval frame ​into which ‌the lay fits ​its ending ‌— Oisín ​and Caílte ​reciting Ireland ​to St. ​Patrick — ‌is preserved ‌in the ​*Acallam na ‌Senórach*, whose ​great witness ​is the ‌fifteenth-century Book ‌of Lismore, ‌with Oxford's ‌Laud Misc. ​610 among ‌its sister ​codices.[^3] Her ​Otherworld has ​no fixed ‌address, and ​that is ​its nature: ​unlike the ‌[[dagda|Dagda]]'s Brú ​na Bóinne, ​where Newgrange ​gives myth ‌a monument, ​Tír na ‌nÓg was ​never mapped ‌onto any ​real island. ‌The material ‌record of ​Niamh is ​the manuscript ​tradition itself ​— and ‌the unbroken ‌popularity of ​her name.[^4]

meditation.body:
Niamh is ​the name ‌of a temptation, ‌and the ​temptation is ​not what it ​first seems. ​She offers beauty, ​youth, and ‌three hundred ​years without a ​wrinkle — ‌and the story's ​verdict is ‌that the offer ​is genuine. ‌Tír na ​nÓg is no ​trap: the ​children are real, ​the delight ​is real, the ‌warning she ​gives him ‌is honest and ​exact. What ‌the lay understands ​is that ‌exemption from ​time is itself ‌a kind ​of exile, and ​that a ‌mortal carries his ‌mortality inside ‌him as ​homesickness. Oisín does ​not fall ‌because the Otherworld ​failed him; ​he falls because ‌Ireland is ​his, and ​a single touch ‌of its ​soil outweighs three ‌centuries of ​paradise.[^1]

Her ​name keeps the ​paradox in ​one syllable. Niamh ‌— radiance, ‌the shining thing ​— is ‌the brightest ​name in the ​Fenian cycle, ‌and she rides ‌it out ‌of the sea ‌to the ​one man ‌whose whole art ​was memory. ​Between them the ​lay poses ‌the question ​it never answers: ​is the ​golden age the ‌land across ​the water where ​nothing ages, ​or the ‌lost Ireland of ​the Fianna ‌that the old ​poet spends ‌his last days ​reciting to ‌a saint? ‌Niamh holds one ​answer. Oisín ​holds the other. ​The white ​horse runs ‌between them, and ‌it does ​not wait.

sources.citation: O'Daly, John, ed. and trans., 'The Lay of Oisin in the Land of the Young', Transactions of the Ossianic Society 4 (1859).

irish-cycles.body:
Niamh belongs ​to the ‌Fenian (or ‌Ossianic) Cycle ​— the body ​of Irish ​narrative that ​gathers around ​[[fionn|Fionn mac Cumhaill]], ‌the Fianna, ​and Fionn's ​poet-son [[oisin|Oisín]] — ‌and not ​to the ‌Mythological Cycle ​of the Túatha ‌Dé Danann, ​though her ​father and ​her country are ​borrowed from ​the older ‌stratum.[^1] The ​cycle's medieval masterpiece, ‌the *Acallam ​na Senórach* ‌(c. 1200), ​established the frame ‌her story ​would inherit: ‌Oisín and ​Caílte, improbably long-lived ​survivors of ‌the Fianna, ‌walking Ireland with ‌St. Patrick ​and reciting ​its heathen ‌golden age to ​the new ​faith.[^2]

The ‌Niamh episode ​itself is the ​cycle's late ‌flowering. Fenian ​lays about ‌Oisín in the ​Land of ​Youth circulated ​in the ​lay tradition collected ‌in *Duanaire ‌Finn*,[^3] but ​the received ‌text is the ​*Laoi Oisín ​ar Thír ‌na nÓg* ascribed ‌to the ‌eighteenth-century Clare ‌poet Mícheál ​Coimín — the ‌fullest and ​most beloved ​version, printed ​by the Ossianic ‌Society in ​1859 and ​carried into ​English by the ‌Revival.[^4] The ​cycle's characteristic ​melancholy — ​the Fianna as ‌a lost ​golden age ‌— finds ​in her story ‌its sharpest ​form: the ‌last Fenian is ‌offered a ​way not ​to age ​at all, and ​gives it ‌up for ‌one sight ​of home.

sources.citation: Koch, John T., ed., Celtic Culture: A Historical Encyclopedia, 5 vols. (Santa Barbara: ABC-CLIO, 2006), s.v. Fenian cycle, Oisín.
Stokes, Whitley, ed. and trans., 'Acallamh na Senórach', Irische Texte, ser. 4, vol. 1 (Leipzig: Hirzel, 1900).
Mac Neill, Eoin, and Gerard Murphy, ed. and trans., Duanaire Finn: The Book of the Lays of Fionn, Irish Texts Society (1908–53).
O'Daly, John, ed. and trans., 'The Lay of Oisin in the Land of the Young', Transactions of the Ossianic Society 4 (1859).

welsh-sources.body:
The ​Welsh corpus ‌preserves no ‌Niamh, and ​the silence ​deserves to ​be recorded ​rather than ​repaired: neither ‌the *Mabinogi* ​nor the ​wider Brythonic ‌tradition knows ​a ‌figure derived ​from the ‌same name, ​and no ​scholar has ​proposed one.[^1]

​What the ​comparison does ‌show is ​instructive by ‌resonance. Niamh's ​traditional ‌father [[manannan|Manannán ​mac Lir]] ‌has a ​secure Welsh ‌cognate in ​[[manawydan|Manawydan fab ​Llŷr]], the ‌patient craftsman ‌of the ‌Third Branch ​— the ​sea-Otherworld's lord ‌on ​both sides ​of the ‌Irish Sea.[^1] ​Her unmatchable ​white horse ‌and her ​sovereignty over ‌the crossing ​find their ​nearest Brythonic ​echo in ​[[rhiannon|Rhiannon]], ‌whose pace ‌no rider ​can overtake ‌and who, ​like Niamh, ​does her ‌own choosing ‌of a ‌mortal man.[^2] ‌And the ​Welsh Otherworld ‌of [[annwn|Annwn]] ​— ​raided in ​*Preiddeu Annwn*, ‌visited in ​the First ​Branch — ​shares Tír ‌na nÓg's ​geography of ​the unreachable: ​a land ‌real enough ​to ‌be named, ​never to ‌be mapped. ​These are ‌kinships of ‌motif, never ​of name; ​the Welsh ​record itself ​is silent, ‌and this ‌edition says ​so.[^1]

sources.citation: Koch, John T., ed., Celtic Culture: A Historical Encyclopedia, 5 vols. (Santa Barbara: ABC-CLIO, 2006), s.v. Manannán mac Lir, Manawydan fab Llŷr, Annwfn.
Mac Cana, Proinsias, Celtic Mythology (London: Hamlyn, 1970), on Rhiannon and the Welsh Otherworld.

inscriptions.body:
No ​inscription names ‌Niamh. ‌**Ogham**, the ​early ​Irish monumental ​script ​of roughly ​the ‌fourth to ​seventh ​centuries, survives ‌on ​some four ‌hundred ​stones bearing ‌mostly ​personal names ​in ​formulaic genitives; ​no ​reading of ‌Niamh ​— or ‌of ​its root ‌*niam* ​— has ‌been ​proposed for ‌any ​of them, ​and ‌none would ‌be ‌expected: ogham ​stones ​mark graves ‌and ​boundaries, not ​the ‌Otherworld.[^1]

The ​epigraphic ​silence is ‌characteristic. ​Niamh is ‌a ​creature of ​the ​manuscript tradition ​whole ‌and entire ‌— ​a medieval ‌name ​for a ​medieval ‌story-world, carried ‌not ‌on stone ‌but ​on vellum ‌and, ​later, on ​the ​paper manuscripts ‌of ​the Fenian ​lays. ​Her only ‌durable ​'inscription' is ​onomastic: ​the name's ‌passage ​from the ‌glossaries' ​*niam*, 'lustre', ‌through ​the lay's ‌golden-haired ‌rider, to ​one ​of the ​most ​popular girls' ‌names ‌in modern ​Ireland.[^2]

sources.citation: McManus, Damian, A Guide to Ogam, Maynooth Monographs 4 (Maynooth: An Sagart, 1991).
Dictionary of the Irish Language (Dublin: Royal Irish Academy, 1913–76; electronic ed. eDIL 2019), s.v. 1 niam.

original-script.body:
The name ​is preserved in ‌medieval Irish ‌manuscripts in the ​Latin alphabet as ​**Níam** — Old ​and Middle ​Irish in Insular ​minuscule — beside ‌the common noun ​*niam*, 'lustre, ​brilliance'; the síneadh ‌fada marks the ​long vowel.[^1] The ‌canonical modern ​Irish spelling **Niamh** ‌writes the lenited ​m with the ​digraph mh ​and drops the ​fada; it is ​this modern form ‌that the ​temple carries.[^1] The ‌earlier monumental alphabet, ​ogham, predates the ‌manuscript tradition, ​but no attestation ‌of the name ​has ever been ‌read on ​an ogham stone; ​the manuscript form ‌is the primary ‌witness.[^2]

The ‌scholarly rendering proceeds ​step by step:

​- Old Irish ‌was written ​in the Latin ​alphabet using Insular ‌minuscule from the ​early medieval ​period; the medieval ‌spelling of the ​name is Níam, ‌with the ​fada on the ​í.
- Modern ​Irish regularized the ​spelling to ‌Niamh, the mh ‌digraph writing the ​lenited m ([vˠ]) ‌— plain ​Latin letters throughout.
​- The canonical ‌modern form therefore ‌requires no ‌diacritic: the Unicode ‌restoration Niamh is ​identical to the ‌ASCII form ​apart from the ​capital.
- The ​temple form is ‌a canonical ​reference to the ​living Irish name, ​not a rescued ‌spelling; nothing ​distinctive is lost ​in ASCII.

One ​caution attaches to ‌the record: ​where the medieval ‌spelling Níam is ​quoted, the fada ‌is the ​manuscripts' own; where ‌the temple and ‌the lay tradition ​write Niamh, ​no accent is ​claimed — the ​two spellings are ‌kept distinct, ‌as the sources ​keep them.[^3]

sources.citation: Dictionary of the Irish Language (Dublin: Royal Irish Academy, 1913–76; electronic ed. eDIL 2019), s.v. 1 niam.
McManus, Damian, A Guide to Ogam, Maynooth Monographs 4 (Maynooth: An Sagart, 1991).
MacKillop, James, A Dictionary of Celtic Mythology (Oxford: Oxford University Press, 1998), s.v. Niamh.
